questions.title: What are the core Kanban principles and how do you visualise work for an engineering team?
questions.quick: Kanban starts from where you are, keeps current roles, and improves in small steps. Its practices are to visualise work, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, create feedback loops and improve collaboratively. I visualise on a board with columns that reflect real stages, such as ready, build, review, test and done, with each card showing owner, type, age and blockers. Work-in-progress limits on columns turn the board into a system that shows bottlenecks.
questions.revision: Visualise work, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, add feedback loops and improve together, starting from the current process.
questions.detailed:
## Principles and practices

Kanban is a method for managing the flow of work. It does not prescribe roles or iterations. You begin with your current process, agree to pursue incremental change and respect existing responsibilities.

| Practice | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Visualise work | Board with columns for each real stage |
| Limit work in progress | A number on each column or swimlane |
| Manage flow | Watch cycle time, ageing and blockers |
| Make policies explicit | Written entry, exit and priority rules |
| Feedback loops | Daily stand-up at the board, reviews, retrospectives |
| Improve collaboratively | Small experiments, measured |

## A useful board

{{diagram:board}}

- **Columns** match how work really flows, including waiting states such as "ready for review".
- **Cards** show an owner, work type, class of service, age in days and a visible blocked marker.
- **Swimlanes** separate expedite work from standard work, or Power Platform from AI items.
- **Policies** sit at the top of each column: what must be true to pull a card in.

## For a team of six to ten

One shared board is enough. Review the board daily, walk it right to left so finishing is prioritised over starting, and avoid creating personal boards.

## Common mistakes

- A board that is only a task list, with no limits or policies.
- Columns for roles ("developer", "tester") instead of stages of work.
- Never updating the board, so it lies.
followUps: How is Kanban different from Scrum?
Why walk the board right to left?
What would you put on a card?

diagrams.title: Kanban board with WIP limits
diagrams.alt: Cards move left to right through Backlog, Ready, Build with a limit of four, Review with a limit of two, Test with a limit of three and Done. An expedite lane sits above the standard lane, and blocked cards are flagged where they sit.

questions.title: What are WIP limits and how do you set and adjust them?
questions.quick: A work-in-progress limit caps how many items can be in a stage at once, so people finish before starting. I start with a number near the team size or a little under for the whole system, then set stage limits from the current counts. When a column is full we help clear it instead of starting new work. I review limits in retrospectives: if cards are often idle and limits never bind, tighten; if the team starves, loosen slightly.
questions.revision: WIP limits cap items per stage so work is finished before more starts; set from current reality, then tighten or loosen using ageing and idle data.
questions.detailed:
## Why limit work

According to Little's Law, average cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput. If throughput stays the same, more parallel work means longer cycle time. Limits expose bottlenecks and reduce context switching.

## Setting an initial limit

| Method | Detail |
|---|---|
| Team-based | About one item per person, or slightly fewer, since pairing reduces demand |
| Current-state | Count items per column now and set the limit just under the usual count |
| Per-column | Smaller limit for review and test to prevent queues |

## What happens at the limit

1. No new card is pulled into a full column.
2. People look right: can I help finish something?
3. If nothing can help, raise a blocker or swarm.
4. Never raise the limit just because the column is full, that defeats the point.

## Adjusting

- **Tighten** if cycle time is long, items age, and limits are never reached.
- **Loosen** if people are idle for long periods and the column upstream is full.
- Change one limit at a time and observe for two weeks.
- Include a per-person limit as a guide if individuals juggle many items.

## Common mistakes

- Setting limits and then ignoring them when work is urgent; use an expedite policy instead.
- Counting only started tasks and not blocked ones.
- Treating the limit as a target to fill.
followUps: What is Little's Law?
What do you do when someone says limits slow them down?
Should blocked items count towards the limit?

questions.title: Which flow metrics do you chart, and how do you read a cumulative flow diagram?
questions.quick: I track cycle time, lead time, throughput, work in progress and work-item age. Cycle time is start to finish on our work, lead time includes the wait before we start. I chart a cycle-time scatterplot with percentile lines, throughput per week, and a cumulative flow diagram. On the diagram, band thickness is work in progress, widening bands signal a bottleneck, flat lines mean nothing finishes, and the horizontal distance approximates lead time.
questions.revision: Chart cycle time scatterplot, throughput, work-item age and a cumulative flow diagram; widening bands show bottlenecks and flat lines show stalled delivery.
questions.detailed:
## Definitions

| Metric | Meaning | Chart |
|---|---|---|
| Lead time | Request to delivery, includes waiting | Scatterplot |
| Cycle time | Work started to finished | Scatterplot with 50th, 85th, 95th percentiles |
| Throughput | Items finished per week | Run chart or histogram |
| Work in progress | Items started and not finished | Line, or CFD band |
| Work-item age | Days since start for unfinished items | Age chart against percentiles |

**Work-item age** is the best early warning: an item older than the 85th percentile of past cycle times is at risk now, before it is late.

## Reading a cumulative flow diagram

{{diagram:cfd}}

| Pattern | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Band widening | More items arriving than leaving that stage | Find the bottleneck and swarm |
| Flat Done line | Nothing delivered | Check blockers and release process |
| Parallel, evenly spaced bands | Stable flow | Keep going |
| Staircase Done line | Batch releases | Release smaller, more often |

## Use percentiles, not averages

Say "85% of items finish in ten days or fewer". This is a usable promise, an average is not.

## Common mistakes

- Reporting average cycle time only.
- Mixing very different work types into one chart.
- Using metrics to compare individuals.
followUps: Why is the 85th percentile more useful than the average?
What does a flat Done line mean?
How is lead time different from cycle time?

diagrams.title: Reading a cumulative flow diagram
diagrams.alt: A cumulative flow diagram stacks bands for backlog, in progress, review and done over time. Vertical thickness of a band is work in progress at that stage, horizontal distance is approximate lead time, a widening review band shows a bottleneck, and a flat done line shows no delivery.

nodes.label: Flat Done line means no delivery

questions.title: How do you manage blockers and set a blocked-work policy?
questions.quick: I make blockers visible: a blocked marker with a reason, an owner who is chasing it, and the date it was blocked. The policy says blocked cards stay in their column and still count toward the limit, so the pain is visible. We review blockers daily, set time thresholds for escalation, for example two days to the lead and five days to the sponsor, and track blocked time by cause. Recurring causes become improvement work.
questions.revision: Mark blocked cards with reason, owner and date, keep them inside WIP limits, review daily, escalate by time thresholds and fix recurring causes.
questions.detailed:
## Policy elements

| Element | Example |
|---|---|
| Definition | Work cannot progress because of something outside the assignee's control |
| Marker | Red flag with reason and chaser name |
| Counting | Stays in column and counts toward the limit |
| Review | Daily at the board, oldest first |
| Escalation | Two days: lead; five days: sponsor or other team's manager |
| Measurement | Blocked days by category |

## Common blocker categories

- Waiting for access or environment.
- Waiting for a decision or requirements.
- Dependency on another team.
- Technical impediment or platform limitation.

## Process

1. Mark the card immediately with a reason.
2. Assign a person to unblock, not just to wait.
3. Discuss at the daily board review.
4. Escalate when the threshold passes.
5. Record blocked time and cause when it clears.

## Improve the system

If access requests are the main cause, agree a service level with the owning team or pre-provision environments. If decisions are slow, schedule a standing decision slot with the product owner.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Moving blocked cards to a "waiting" column, which hides them and frees WIP.
- Starting new work while blocked items sit untouched.
- Escalating late or emotionally, without data.
followUps: Why should blocked items still count toward WIP?
How do you escalate a blocker owned by another team?
What do you do if a card is blocked for weeks?

questions.title: What are classes of service and how do you use them to prioritise?
questions.quick: Classes of service group work by the cost of delay and give each group an explicit policy. Typical classes are expedite for critical issues, fixed date for hard deadlines, standard for most work, and intangible for improvements with no urgent date. Each has rules about limits, how it is pulled and what service level to expect. This makes prioritisation transparent, because stakeholders see the rules instead of arguing item by item.
questions.revision: Classes of service group work by cost of delay, such as expedite, fixed date, standard and intangible, each with explicit limits and service levels.
questions.detailed:
## Typical classes

| Class | Cost of delay | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Expedite | Immediate, severe | One at a time, may break limits, swarm |
| Fixed date | Steps up at a deadline | Pull so it finishes before the date with a safety margin |
| Standard | Linear, moderate | Pull by value and age |
| Intangible | Later, hard to quantify | Reserved share of capacity, such as 15% |

## Using them

1. Agree definitions with the product owner so classification is not subjective.
2. Set a **capacity allocation**, for example 10% expedite, 20% fixed date, 55% standard, 15% intangible.
3. Give each class a service-level expectation, such as standard items finish within ten days 85% of the time.
4. Review the mix monthly. Many expedites mean upstream quality problems.

## Prioritising within a class

Use cost of delay divided by size, sometimes called weighted shortest job first, or simple value against effort. Include age so old items do not starve.

## For AI and Power Platform work

A fixed-date item might be a compliance change or a campaign launch. Intangibles include evaluation harness improvements, automated tests and platform housekeeping that prevent future incidents.

## Common mistakes

- Classifying everything as urgent.
- No capacity reserved for intangibles, so debt grows.
- Changing class after the fact to justify a decision.
followUps: How do you stop everything becoming expedite?
What is cost of delay?
How do you choose capacity allocation?

questions.title: How do you balance incident work against planned delivery?
questions.quick: I measure how much capacity incidents really consume, then reserve that share as a buffer in planning. Genuine critical incidents use the expedite lane with a strict limit; lower-severity issues enter the normal flow by class of service. I rotate an on-call or support role so the whole team is not interrupted. I report the interruption cost to stakeholders, and I invest in the causes, since repeated incidents mean quality debt.
questions.revision: Reserve measured capacity for incidents, use an expedite lane for critical ones, rotate a support role, and invest in removing recurring causes.
questions.detailed:
## Capacity view

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| Measure | Last three months: share of throughput spent on unplanned work |
| Reserve | Set capacity buffer near that share, for example 20% |
| Triage | Severity levels decide expedite versus normal flow |
| Protect | Rotating incident owner absorbs interruptions |
| Report | Planned versus unplanned items finished |

## Triage rules

- **Severity 1:** outage or data risk: expedite lane, swarm, communications.
- **Severity 2:** major degradation: next pull, within a day.
- **Severity 3:** minor: standard backlog.

## Protecting planned work

With a rotating support person, the others keep their focus. When the incident load exceeds the buffer, say so with data and ask the product owner to choose what slips. Do not silently extend hours.

## Reduce the load

- Review incidents for recurring causes.
- Add monitoring so issues are found before users find them.
- Automate the common fixes and write runbooks.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Planning to 100% capacity.
- Letting every engineer drop everything for every alert.
- Not tracking incident work, so its cost stays invisible.
followUps: How big should the buffer be?
How do you rotate support fairly?
How do you report interruption cost?

questions.title: How do you plan capacity and forecast releases using throughput?
questions.quick: I use historical throughput, items finished per week, instead of estimates. For a release I count the remaining items, allow for expected growth and splitting, and run a Monte Carlo simulation: randomly sample from past weekly throughput thousands of times to see how many weeks it takes. The result is a distribution, so I say there is an 85% chance we finish by a date. I update the forecast as items complete and the data changes.
questions.revision: Forecast from historical throughput with Monte Carlo sampling to give date ranges with confidence levels, updating as items finish.
questions.detailed:
## Method

1. **Collect** weekly throughput for the last 8 to 12 weeks.
2. **Count** remaining items, adding an allowance for work not yet discovered or items that split.
3. **Simulate:** sample a week's throughput at random from history, repeat until the remaining items are done, record the number of weeks, repeat several thousand times.
4. **Read** the distribution at 50%, 85% and 95%.

| Percentile | Reading |
|---|---|
| 50% | Coin toss, not a commitment |
| 85% | Common planning figure |
| 95% | Conservative, for fixed dates |

A simple spreadsheet or small script is enough. You can also ask "how many items by this date?", which reverses the question.

## Capacity planning

- Throughput already includes holidays, incidents and meetings, if history covers them.
- Adjust for known changes, such as leave or a specialist leaving.
- Keep items **similar in size**: slice so most are a few days, since the method counts items.

## Communicating

Share ranges and assumptions: "85% confident by mid-March, assuming scope grows by 15% and team size stays the same." Re-forecast every fortnight.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Using too little history or a different team's data.
- Forgetting scope growth.
- Treating the 50% date as a promise.
followUps: Why count items instead of story points?
What if you have very little history?
How do you handle one huge item?

questions.title: How do you manage dependencies across global teams and time zones?
questions.quick: I make dependencies visible early, on the board and in a dependency map, with the other team, the date needed and a named contact on each side. I agree interfaces and contracts first so teams can work in parallel with mocks. Handoffs use written, complete requests and service levels that fit time zones, with a short overlap window for decisions. Dependencies age on the board and go to the risk log and escalation when overdue.
questions.revision: Make dependencies visible with owners and dates, agree contracts so teams work in parallel, use written handoffs across time zones and escalate when they age.
questions.detailed:
## Practices

| Practice | Benefit |
|---|---|
| Dependency map reviewed regularly | Surprises found early |
| Named contact on each side | Fast answers |
| Agreed interface or API contract with mocks | Parallel work |
| Written, complete requests | No waiting for clarification overnight |
| Overlap window for decisions | Cuts round trips |
| Dependency cards with age | Visible on the board |

## Time-zone rules

- Ask the complete question with context and a proposed answer, so the other side can reply with yes or no.
- Use shared environments or documented environment contracts.
- Keep a shared calendar of freezes and release windows.

## Escalation

A dependency card is flagged when it is older than agreed, for example five working days. The owner raises it with the other team's lead, then the sponsors, using the risk memo format.

## Reduce dependencies

Prefer reusable components, self-service platforms and clear ownership. Where a team is a recurring bottleneck, propose a service level or an embedded engineer.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Discovering dependencies at integration time.
- Assuming a verbal agreement is enough.
- Waiting passively for the other team.
followUps: How do you work in parallel before the other team delivers?
What if the other team has different priorities?
How do you track dependencies on the board?

questions.title: What quality gates and definition of done do you set for Power Platform and AI work?
questions.quick: I use gates the pipeline can check and a definition of done the team agrees. For Power Platform: work in a managed solution, no hard-coded environment values, connection references and environment variables, automated solution checks, tests where possible, security roles reviewed and data-loss-prevention policies respected. For AI: an evaluation set with agreed pass thresholds, versioned prompts, safety and data-privacy checks, monitoring and cost controls. Every item also needs review, documentation and a rollback path.
questions.revision: Combine automated pipeline gates and a team-agreed definition of done covering solution hygiene, tests, security, AI evaluation, monitoring and rollback.
questions.detailed:
## Gates in the delivery path

{{diagram:gates}}

## Definition of done

| Area | Criteria |
|---|---|
| Solution hygiene | Managed solution, connection references, environment variables, no secrets in flows |
| Automated checks | Solution checker with no critical findings, linting, unit tests where available |
| Testing | Test cases and evidence, user acceptance sign-off for user-facing change |
| Security | Roles and sharing reviewed, data-loss-prevention policy compliant, least privilege |
| AI quality | Evaluation set passed at the agreed threshold, prompts versioned, groundedness and safety checks |
| Operations | Monitoring and alerts, runbook, cost limits, rollback path |
| Knowledge | Decision record, user guidance, review completed |

## AI-specific points

- Regression test prompts and retrieval against a fixed evaluation set when anything changes, including the model version.
- Track cost per request and set budgets.
- Human-in-the-loop for actions with real consequences.

## Applying it

Keep the list short enough to follow. Tier it by risk: a small internal flow needs fewer gates than a customer-facing AI assistant.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Done meaning "works on my environment".
- Skipping evaluations because AI output "looks fine".
- Gates that are manual and so skipped under pressure.
followUps: How do you test a low-code flow automatically?
How do you set an AI evaluation threshold?
How do you keep the definition of done from becoming a burden?

diagrams.title: Quality gates before production
diagrams.alt: A change moves from build to automated checks, then peer review, then test environment evaluation including AI evaluation and security review, then approval and release with monitoring. Failing any gate returns the work to build.

questions.title: How do you balance research spikes with committed delivery?
questions.quick: I treat a spike as a timeboxed experiment with a question, a time limit and an expected output, such as a decision or a recommendation, not as code to ship. I allocate a fixed share of capacity, say ten to fifteen percent, so exploration does not steal from commitments. Spikes go on the board as their own class, they are limited in number, and they end with a short demo and a decision: adopt, adapt or drop.
questions.revision: Run spikes as timeboxed experiments with a question and decision output, within a capped share of capacity, ending in adopt, adapt or drop.
questions.detailed:
## Spike charter

| Item | Example |
|---|---|
| Question | Can retrieval over our policy documents reach the accuracy we need? |
| Timebox | Three days |
| Output | Findings, a recommendation, rough effort estimate |
| Success criteria | Evaluation score on a small test set |
| Decision owner | Product owner and lead |

## Balancing

- Reserve a capacity share, for example 10% to 15%, as an intangible or exploration class.
- Limit to one or two spikes at a time.
- Do not extend a spike silently: if the box ends, decide to stop or fund a second one explicitly.
- Throw away spike code or rebuild properly; do not promote it to production by drift.

## For AI work

AI is uncertain, so run small spikes early for feasibility, such as accuracy, latency and cost. Share the results with stakeholders so commitments are based on evidence.

## Review

Hold a short demo, record the decision and any new items created. If spikes often overrun, the questions are too big: split them.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Open-ended exploration with no output.
- Committing delivery dates before the spike answers feasibility.
- Shipping prototype code.
followUps: How do you timebox something unpredictable?
What if the spike gives an inconclusive answer?
How do you explain spikes to stakeholders?

questions.title: How do you drive continuous improvement with retrospectives and flow reviews?
questions.quick: I use two rhythms. A fortnightly retrospective looks at what the team felt: what worked, what hurt, and one or two actions with owners. A monthly flow review looks at the data: cycle time percentiles, throughput, ageing, blocked time and forecast accuracy, to find the bottleneck. I pick a small number of experiments, state the expected effect, run them for a few weeks and check the metrics. Actions go on the board like any other work.
questions.revision: Hold fortnightly retrospectives for team experience and monthly flow reviews for data, choose few experiments, track them on the board and measure effect.
questions.detailed:
## Two complementary meetings

| Meeting | Focus | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retrospective | People and process | Team observations | One or two experiments with owners |
| Flow review | System performance | Cycle time, throughput, ageing, blocked time | Bottleneck and limit or policy changes |

## Retrospective format

1. Check last time's actions.
2. Gather observations: what helped, what hurt.
3. Choose the biggest issue and find root causes.
4. Agree one or two experiments, with an owner and a date.

## Flow review agenda

- Cycle time scatterplot and percentiles: any change?
- Items that aged beyond the 85th percentile and why.
- Where the cumulative flow bands widen.
- Blocked time by category.
- Forecast accuracy: were we inside the range?

## Making it stick

- Write each experiment as a hypothesis: "If we limit review to two items, review wait will fall below one day."
- Put actions on the board and review them first next time.
- Celebrate improvements and stop experiments that do not work.

## In the interview

Use these points in an interview by giving one concrete, hypothetical example and the measure you would watch afterwards. State the policy first, then the data that shows whether it works, then how you would adjust it with the team. Keep the explanation simple enough that a product owner or sponsor can repeat it, and mention who decides when there is a trade-off, since agreed ownership prevents disputes under pressure. Review the arrangement regularly so it does not become stale.

## Common mistakes

- Repeating the same complaints with no actions.
- Too many actions at once.
- Data without the team's context, or context without data.
followUps: How do you keep retrospectives fresh?
What if actions are never completed?
Which metric tells you the process is improving?
